AI infra startup Modal raises $750 mn at $15.7 bn valuation
Supriya Roy / Oct 14, 2026, 23:20 IST
Save
Comments
Share
Aa
+ Text Size
Small
Medium
Large Print
Modal co-founders (L-R) Erik Bernhardsson and Akshat Bubna
BENGALURU : AI infrastructure startup Modal Labs, co-founded by Delhi-raised computer scientist and Olympiad gold medallist Akshat Bubna, has raised $750 million that values the company at $15.7 billion. The fundraise comes as the five-year-old company crossed $1 billion in annualised revenue run rate, fuelled by growing demand for infrastructure that powers AI applications. The latest valuation is more than three times the $4.6 billion Modal was valued at in May this year, when it raised $355 million in a Series C round. The company’s valuation has risen more than 14-fold since September 2025, when it was worth $1.1 billion. Accel led the latest round, with Kleiner Perkins joining as an investor. Existing backers Menlo Ventures, General Catalyst, Redpoint, Lux Capital and Bain Capital Ventures also participated, the company said on Wednesday. Modal said usage of its platform had tripled in the five months since its previous funding round, while the business had grown more than 15-fold year-on-year. Its annualised run rate, which reflects the pace of revenue extrapolated over a year rather than revenue earned in the preceding 12 months, has climbed from about $300 million in May to over $1 billion.
Founded in 2021 by Bubna and Swedish engineer Erik Bernhardsson, Modal provides computing infrastructure that allows companies to develop, run and scale AI applications without having to manage their own servers or computing hardware. Its platform now draws capacity from more than 20 cloud providers, allowing developers to access computing power as demand rises or falls. One of Modal’s fastest-growing businesses is Sandboxes, a product that allows AI agents to execute code in isolated environments. Launched in 2023, the product alone has reached a $300 million annualised run rate, the company said. Modal claims it has launched nearly three billion such environments to date and can support up to one million running simultaneously. The surge reflects growing adoption of AI coding agents, which need computing environments to execute programs, test results and carry out tasks. articles.title: AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding
articles.snippet: AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
UPDATED 22:11 EDT / OCTOBER 20 2026
AI
AI infrastructure management software startup ASI hits $3B valuation after raising $325M in funding
by Mike Wheatley
An artificial intelligence startup called ASI Inc. , which builds complex models of air traffic and energy grids, said today it has scored $325 million in a Series C funding, bringing its valuation to a cool $3 billion.
The round was led by Spark Capital and joined by participants including Citadel Securities, Craft Ventures, Meritech Capital, Energy Impact Partners and Andreessen Horowitz.
The startup, which used to be known as Air Space Intelligence, is an AI company that develops frontier models designed to model physical reality and simulate future scenarios, so that its customers can plan and orchestrate how they operate critical infrastructure in real time.
It caters to companies in the aviation , defense and energy industries. For instance, it works with the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines such as United Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc. to simulate and predict what’s happening in air space, so they can plan their flight operations. It gives pilots and air traffic controllers a way to plan ahead, reduce delays and increase flight safety and efficiency.
In addition, ASI works with the U.S. Army, U.S. Air Force and others, providing them with AI-driven command-and-control software that’s used to manage their daily operations. It also helps companies in the energy sector, including grid operators, enabling them to simulate their grid operations and plan for surges in demand.
ASI founder and Chief Executive Phillip Buckendorf (pictured) said he believes that future economic growth will be dependent on giving the people who run the country’s most critical infrastructure the ability to predict and forecast scenarios ahead of time, so they can avoid failures. “While the broader tech ecosystem spent hundreds of billions teaching AI to manipulate words and generate text, ASI is deeply focused on AI systems that can manage and control physical assets,” he stressed. “This capital ensures ASI scales as America’s engine: the automated nervous system keeping the country running.”
While hundreds of billions have been spent teaching AI to manipulate words and generate videos, ASI builds AI systems that can manage and control critical physical infrastructure – where there is zero margin for error.
Today we announced our $325M Series C to scale America’s… pic.twitter.com/l133h8H92E
— ASI (@AirSpaceIntel) October 20, 2026
The round follows a significant customer win for ASI. In June, it signed an $875 million multiyear agreement with the FAA to manage future air traffic across the U.S. with its AI platform. Impressively, it won the 12-year contract ahead of bigger and better known rivals such as Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SE, which both made aggressive bids, according to Bloomberg .
In air traffic scenarios, ASI’s system combines data from flight paths, real-time air traffic, weather and controller staffing to predict congestion and devise ways to get around problems and avoid delays. The FAA implemented the software at Dulles International Airport in Washington DC last month, and plans to expand it to all major U.S. airports in future.

Indian startups raise $2.9 Bn in Q3 2026 as EV, AI drive funding
Indian startups raised less than $3 billion in funding in Q3 2026, down from $3.5 billion in Q2 and $3.87 billion in Q1. The quarter saw fewer large funding rounds,
Shashank Pathak & Mukul Manchanda
01 Oct 2026
15:40
IST
Follow Us
New Update
Indian startups raised less than $3 billion in funding in Q3 2026, down from $3.5 billion in Q2 and $3.87 billion in Q1. The quarter saw fewer large funding rounds, with Simple Energy leading the pack with a $182 million raise. The round also made Simple Energy the third-largest funded Indian electric two-wheeler OEM. Physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which has deep Indian roots and a major research and development centre in Bengaluru, raised another $150 million . Emergent, River Mobility, Navi, Slice and Pixxel also secured more than $100 million each during the quarter.
Despite the decline in overall funding, early-stage deals crossed the $1 billion mark in Q3. The quarter also saw six startup listings, including NSE, Rentomojo, Molbio, Milky Mist, Leap India and Purple Style Labs. Six startups shut down operations during the quarter.
[ Overview ]
According to data compiled by Entrackr, Indian startups raised approximately $2.9 billion in funding during the third quarter of 2026. This amount included 46 growth and late-stage deals totalling $1.89 billion, along with 194 early-stage deals worth $1.01 billion. Additionally, there were 26 undisclosed deals during the period.
[Q-o-Q and M-o-M trend]
Q3 2026 saw a modest recovery in startup funding compared to the same quarter last year. Total funding rose to $2.9 billion from $2.78 billion in Q3 2025, but remained below the $4 billion recorded in Q3 2024. September emerged as a strong month for funding, as startups raised more than $1 billion for the third time in 2026. February and June were the previous two months to cross the $1 billion mark, with each recording around $2 billion in funding. The September uptick helped Q3 close above the funding level recorded in the year-ago quarter.
[Top 15 growth-stage deals]
In Q3 2026, India’s top 15 growth and late-stage deals reflected strong investor interest in mobility, AI and fintech, along with bets across consumer and deeptech sectors. Simple Energy topped the list after raising $182 million in its Series C round, followed by physical AI startup SiMa.ai, which secured $150 million in Series C funding. AI startup Emergent raised $130 million , while electric two-wheeler maker River Mobility secured $120 million. Fintech firms Navi and Slice raised $100 million each, while electric mobility platform Yulu followed with $93 million. EV maker Ultraviolette raised $85 million, while AI startups Ema and Sarvam AI secured $77 million and $74 million, respectively. Wearable tech startup Ultrahuman raised $70 million, while The Pizza Bakery secured $56 million. Healthtech startup Nua raised $50 million, followed by Third Wave Coffee at $43 million and aerospace and defence company Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group at $40 million.
[Top 15 early-stage deals]
Early-stage activity remained strong in Q3 2026, led by Pixxel’s $100 million Series A and Airbound’s $37 million Series A. Yuma Energy followed with $35 million, while Centricity and InRisk Labs raised $30 million and $27 million, respectively. articles.title: Nuvacore startup raises hundreds of millions at $2.5 billion valuation for new data center processor
articles.snippet: Nuvacore startup raises hundreds of millions at $2.5 billion valuation for new data center processor ET CIO
articles.text:
Next-Gen Technologies
2 min read
Nuvacore startup raises hundreds of millions at $2.5 billion valuation for new data center processor
Nuvacore, a six-month-old startup, is raising significant funds for its central processor development aimed at data centers. The company plans to optimize chip design for common data center and AI computations, avoiding traditional architecture limitations. Founded by former Apple executive Gerard Williams, Nuvacore has already secured previous funding led by Sequoia Capital. Investor interest in semiconductor startups has increased significantly in recent months, surpassing previous funding totals.
Reuters
Published On Oct 10, 2026 at 08:09 AM IST
Set ETCIO as your preferred source on Google

Share on Facebook
Six-month-old microchip startup Nuvacore , which does not yet have a product, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a roughly $2.5 billion valuation to develop a new central processor designed for data centers , according to two people familiar with the fundraising.
Nuvacore is seeking to raise the funds as the appetite for central processors has swollen due to the thirst for data-crunching capacity to power chatbots such as Anthropic's Claude. CPUs perform vital functions as traffic controllers for Nvidia's AI chips and run autonomous AI software known as agents.
The roughly $2.5 billion valuation has not been previously reported. The Information reported previously that Nuvacore was raising $200 million or more. The funding round has not closed, and the people cautioned that the valuation and size of the capital raise could change.
Advt
Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, which use x86 technology, have long dominated the data center CPU market. Companies designing chips based on Arm's technology - found inside Amazon and Microsoft custom CPUs - have also attempted to make inroads in the data center market.
Nuvacore has not yet developed a product. Last month, it described an unconventional design strategy: to build the core functionality of the chip before committing to an architecture such as the x86 used by Intel and AMD, or Arm, which is used in most mobile phones.
The design strategy will allow the company's engineers to avoid the limitations and requirements of specific architectures and optimize a design for the type of computations that are most common in data centers and AI infrastructure, Nuvacore said.
Nuvacore declined to comment.
The San Jose, California-based startup was founded by renowned engineers Gerard Williams, John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan. Williams, a former Apple executive, sold a prior startup called Nuvia to Qualcomm for $1.4 billion in 2021.
Nuvacore earlier this year announced a seed funding round led by Sequoia Capital. It joins a series of young chip startups that have sought billion-dollar valuations before releasing a product as investor appetite for AI hardware companies has returned.
Over the past decade, Silicon Valley venture capital firms have taken much less interest in hardware than software because of hardware's longer development cycles, higher capital needs and the industry's cyclical demand.

Investors put about $10.7 billion into semiconductor startups in the first five months of 2026, already outpacing the $12.2 billion raised globally in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

AI startups announced about $2.42 billion in primary funding across 19 rounds of $20 million or more between October 12 and October 18, 2026. Modal Labs’ $750 million Series D was the largest round, at about 31% of the total.
The largest AI acquisition was much smaller. Rocket Software bought Israeli startup Geniez AI in a deal Calcalist estimated at up to $100 million. Neither company disclosed the price.
North American companies raised $1.28 billion, or 53% of the total. Four Chinese startups raised about $943 million (39%), two European startups raised $157 million, and Israel’s Pluto Security raised $42 million.

A fund close is money a venture firm collects from its own backers to invest later, so it is not counted in the startup total. No employee share sale or other secondary deal qualified this week.
